title: Proprioception: Sensing the Body's Own Position

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The main sensory contributors to limb-position estimates are {{c1::muscle spindles}}.
cards.back: They signal muscle length.
cards.quote: Your sense of limb position is an estimate, built mainly from muscle spindle signals of muscle length, with skin, joint and motor-command signals added.
cards.section: The illusion, and the rule it reveals

cards.front: Why can tendon vibration make a stationary, unseen limb seem to move?
cards.back: Vibration drives spindle endings. Their firing carries no label of its cause, so the brain can interpret the extra activity as muscle stretch.
cards.quote: A spindle's firing carries no label saying what caused it.
cards.section: The illusion, and the rule it reveals

cards.front: In separate trials, an unseen elbow stays still while either its biceps or triceps tendon is vibrated. Biceps lengthens with extension; triceps lengthens with flexion. What usual perceptual biases follow, and why?
cards.back: Biceps vibration biases toward extension; triceps vibration biases toward flexion. In each trial, the extra spindle activity is usually read as lengthening of the vibrated muscle.
cards.quote: Subjects judged the elbow to be where it would have been if the vibrated muscle had been stretched:
cards.section: The illusion, and the rule it reveals

cards.front: Why does increased spindle firing not uniquely determine the perceived position of a limb?
cards.back: Position is a combined estimate: motor state, stimulation history and other sensory inputs also matter. Extra spindle firing therefore predicts a usual bias, not an invariant percept.
cards.quote: a typical direction, not a percept that every rise in spindle firing must produce, since motor state, stimulation history and other inputs matter.
cards.section: The illusion, and the rule it reveals

cards.front: A muscle spindle's {{c1::primary (Ia) ending}} is especially sensitive to small, rapid stretches.
cards.quote: Its primary (Ia) ending is especially sensitive to small, rapid stretches.
cards.section: The illusion, and the rule it reveals

cards.front: How do Ia and II spindle endings differ in their coding of static length and changing length?
cards.back: Both signal static length and changes in length. Ia endings have greater rate sensitivity; Ia is not a velocity-only signal.
cards.quote: Both signal static muscle length, and Ia endings add sensitivity to the rate of change of length.

cards.front: Muscle spindle sensory endings sit on the {{c1::central region}} of the intrafusal fibres.
cards.quote: The sensory endings sit on their central region.

cards.front: How does gamma motor drive increase muscle spindle gain?
cards.back: Gamma drive contracts the intrafusal poles, stretching the sensory middle and increasing ending activity. This changes how strongly the endings respond to a given stretch.
cards.quote: gamma drive contracts the poles, the poles stretch the middle, and the endings there fire more.

cards.front: What does the Ib afferent of a Golgi tendon organ report?
cards.back: Force from motor units in series with the organ.
cards.quote: It is highly sensitive to contraction of the motor units in series with it, so it reports force from those units.

cards.front: Motor units in series with a Golgi tendon organ contract more strongly while muscle length is held fixed. What happens to its Ib signal, and why?
cards.back: The force signal increases because the organ is sensitive to contraction of those motor units. Fixed muscle length does not make this a zero-force condition.
cards.quote: It is highly sensitive to contraction of the motor units in series with it, so it reports force from those units.

cards.front: During passive finger and thumb rotation in the human joint-afferent study, where did most joint afferents fire?
cards.back: Near the limits of joint rotation, rather than throughout the range; there were exceptions.
cards.quote: Most joint afferents fired near the limits of rotation, not across the range.

cards.front: A human hand joint afferent is quiet during midrange rotation. Does this show that position information from that region is absent?
cards.back: No. A single joint afferent cannot represent the whole population: some joint afferents responded throughout the range, and muscle and skin signals also contribute.
cards.quote: three tonically active afferents responded throughout the physiological range

cards.front: The mechanically activated channel identified as the principal proprioceptive transducer in mice is {{c1::Piezo2}}.
cards.quote: A candidate is Piezo2, a mechanically activated channel,
cards.section: The transducer: Piezo2 on the stretch line

cards.front: In a conditional mouse deletion, how does a Cre driver remove a floxed Piezo2 gene?
cards.back: Cre recombinase removes the gene flanked by its target sites in cells reached by the driver, including their descendants.
cards.quote: it removes the gene in the cells the driver reaches, including their descendants.
cards.section: The transducer: Piezo2 on the stretch line

cards.front: Why did agreement between Pvalb-Cre and HoxB8-Cre Piezo2 deletions strengthen the mouse transduction evidence?
cards.back: The drivers reach different off-target cells. Their shared phenotype is more convincing than a result from either driver alone, although neither targets only proprioceptors.
cards.quote: Two drivers with different off-target cells make a shared result more convincing.
cards.section: The transducer: Piezo2 on the stretch line

cards.front: Piezo2 is present at mouse proprioceptor endings, and mechanical indentation evokes rapidly adapting currents in labelled sensory cell bodies. What additional experiment tests whether the ending needs Piezo2 for stretch signalling?
cards.back: Delete Piezo2 and record sensory firing during stretch of an isolated muscle-nerve preparation. The sharp reduction in stretch-evoked firing supports a functional requirement beyond mere protein localisation.
cards.quote: Stretch-evoked firing was sharply reduced, with either Cre line.
cards.section: The transducer: Piezo2 on the stretch line

cards.front: Why is Piezo2 called the principal, rather than the proven sole, proprioceptive transducer in mice?
cards.back: Deletion sharply reduced stretch responses, but some remained. Incomplete deletion could explain the residue; it neither proves nor rules out another channel.
cards.quote: the residue does not prove a second channel, and it does not rule one out.
cards.section: The transducer: Piezo2 on the stretch line

cards.front: In the mouse sensory-cell recordings, 23 of 25 labelled neurons had rapidly adapting currents. What percentage of the sample is this, and does it estimate the percentage of all proprioceptors?
cards.back: 100 × 23/25 = 92% of the labelled sample. It is not an estimate for all proprioceptors: parvalbumin labels some other neurons too.
cards.quote: Parvalbumin labels proprioceptors and some other neurons, so this is not 92% of proprioceptors.

cards.front: Assume a mechanically activated current decays from its peak as exp(-t/tau), with tau = 5.6 ms. What percentage of peak current remains after 20 ms?
cards.back: Fraction = exp(-20/5.6) = exp(-3.571) ≈ 0.028; about 3% remains. This assumes a single exponential decay.
cards.quote: Assume the current decays as a single exponential from its peak with tau = 5.6 ms.

cards.front: Assume the mouse sensory-cell current decays as exp[-t/(5.6 ms)]. What fraction remains after 1 s, and how can Piezo2 deletion still reduce spindle firing during a held stretch?
cards.back: 1 s = 1000 ms; exp(-1000/5.6) is about 10^-78, effectively zero. The rule is measurement-specific: cultured cell-body current inactivation is not spindle spike adaptation. Deletion shows Piezo2 is needed for held firing, but the full sustaining pathway remains unsettled.
cards.quote: This is a current in a cell body in culture, not a current at a spindle ending.

cards.front: In adult mouse muscle-nerve preparations, added glutamate raised held-stretch firing, while reduced vesicular glutamate packaging impaired it. What conclusion is supported about sustained spindle firing?
cards.back: Vesicle-released glutamate contributes to the held response. These perturbations support a contribution, not a complete explanation of how Piezo2 activation leads to sustained firing.
cards.quote: So vesicle-released glutamate has experimental support as a contributor to the held response,

cards.front: What everyday tasks could the two reported people with inactivating PIEZO2 variants still perform?
cards.back: Walking, talking and writing, although one walked only with support.
cards.quote: they could still perform tasks such as walking, talking and writing, though one walked only with support.

cards.front: A person with greatly reduced proprioceptive input reaches accurately by watching the arm. Visual feedback is then removed. What happens to reaching accuracy, and why?
cards.back: Accuracy is expected to fall markedly because vision was compensating for missing position information. The deficit does not by itself imply loss of motor output.
cards.quote: With the stretch lines silent, vision has to do much of the work of position sense.

cards.front: People with PIEZO2 loss and I.W., who lost large-fibre sensation, both relied heavily on sight for movement. Do these cases isolate spindle loss as the cause of every deficit?
cards.back: No. The population-input rule requires considering other sensory losses: PIEZO2 loss also affects touch, and I.W. lost all large-fibre input. Their shared visual dependence supports compensation for sensory loss, but cannot assign each deficit selectively to spindles.
cards.quote: Neither case is a selective silencing of spindles, since PIEZO2 loss also affects touch and I.W. lost all large-fibre input.

cards.front: Which sensations remained in I.W. despite loss of light touch and proprioception below the neck?
cards.back: Pain, heat, cold and the sense of muscular fatigue.
cards.quote: He lacked light touch and proprioception below the neck but kept pain, heat, cold and the sense of muscular fatigue.

cards.front: Why does I.W.'s inability to make novel movements without sight not demonstrate complete motor loss?
cards.back: He could still hold a posture or continue simple repetitive movement. This preserved movement separates the sensory deficit from complete loss of motor capacity.
cards.quote: In their testing no novel movement was possible without visual feedback, though he could hold a posture or continue a simple repetitive movement.

cards.front: A defect in one tissue caused by gene loss in another tissue is called a {{c1::non-autonomous}} effect.
cards.quote: An effect is non-autonomous when the defect appears in one tissue
cards.section: What else the line is for: the skeleton

cards.front: In mice, deleting Piezo2 with Pvalb-Cre produced scoliosis in some animals; deleting it in the tested bone-forming or cartilage-forming lineages did not. What tissue-level interpretation follows?
cards.back: The results support a non-autonomous role for proprioceptive Piezo2 in alignment at the ages tested. They do not identify the intervening pathway, and Pvalb-Cre is not exclusive to proprioceptors.
cards.quote: proprioceptive Piezo2 acts on the skeleton through a route that does not need Piezo2 inside the bone cells tested.
cards.section: What else the line is for: the skeleton

cards.front: Why does normal-looking spine histology at P10 not rule out a later skeletal effect of mouse Piezo2 deletion?
cards.back: The observations are age-specific: P10 histology showed no apparent difference, but scoliosis appeared by P60 in some animals. An early negative observation does not exclude later change.
cards.quote: Spine histology at P10 showed no apparent differences from controls in bone, cartilage or surrounding soft tissue.
cards.section: What else the line is for: the skeleton

cards.front: Why do skeletal abnormalities in people with PIEZO2 loss not identify the causal tissue in those people?
cards.back: The human cases show association. Mouse tissue-targeted deletions support a mouse non-autonomous role, but do not establish the causal tissue in human families.
cards.quote: Human cases show association, not the causal tissue.
cards.section: What else the line is for: the skeleton

cards.front: How would you test whether mouse skeletal alignment needs proprioceptor Piezo2 during an early postnatal window or also after alignment is established?
cards.back: Induce proprioceptor deletion early or after alignment; compare serial CT at matched ages with littermate controls and an independent driver. The timing rule requires equally complete deletion and equally long follow-up: curvature only after early deletion supports a postnatal window.
cards.quote: If only the early deletion gives scoliosis, and the late deletion is shown to be as complete and is followed as long,

cards.front: An equally complete Piezo2 deletion after mouse skeletal alignment also causes curvature. Does this establish a continuous requirement for feedback throughout adulthood?
cards.back: It establishes a requirement after alignment, not continuous need at every adult age. By the timing rule, deletions at more ages or reversible silencing are needed to test continuity.
cards.quote: deletions at more ages, or reversible silencing, would show whether the need is continuous.

cards.front: Suppose mouse Piezo2 deletion, proprioceptor silencing and proprioceptor loss produce different spinal effects. What comparison would distinguish altered transduction from effects beyond neuronal firing?
cards.back: Match timing, targeted cells and CT measures; verify complete silencing. The channel-versus-cell rule makes deletion–silencing differences candidates for residual transduction or incomplete deletion. Extra effects of cell loss beyond complete silencing motivate testing structural or trophic roles.
cards.quote: First verify that silencing abolishes firing, and match the timing and targeted population across manipulations.

cards.front: Why is a spindle-based estimate of limb position insufficient to explain force and heaviness?
cards.back: Position and force use different information. Tendon organs report force, and a sense of effort associated with motor command also contributes to force and heaviness.
cards.quote: Tendon organs report force, and a sense of effort that comes with the motor command contributes too, as I.W.'s weight test showed.

cards.front: Opposing tendons at an unseen, stationary elbow are vibrated together. What can happen to the movement illusion, and why?
cards.back: The illusion can largely cancel. Opposing muscle signals can counterbalance in the position estimate, so the single-tendon rule cannot simply be applied independently to each muscle.
cards.quote: Vibrating opposing muscles together can largely cancel the illusion

cards.front: A stationary arm is tested with biceps tendon vibration. A researcher predicts exactly 40 degrees of error because an earlier experiment reached that value. Is that magnitude justified, and why?
cards.back: No fixed magnitude is justified. The rule predicts a usual direction; 40 degrees was reached during contraction in one experiment, not established as a standard error.
cards.quote: The 40 degrees was the error during contraction in one experiment, not a standard size.

cards.front: A model assumes that perceived elbow-movement velocity rises monotonically with tendon-vibration frequency. How do the reported frequency-series results test it?
cards.back: They contradict monotonic increase over the tested range: perceived velocity rose to about 70 to 80 Hz in a 10 to 120 Hz series, then fell.
cards.quote: the perceived velocity of movement rose up to about 70 to 80 Hz in a 10 to 120 Hz series before falling.
cards.section: How vibration frequency shapes the illusion

cards.front: Why did glutamate and PCCG-13 effects on rat spindle endings not establish a specific glutamate receptor?
cards.back: The pharmacology supported endogenous glutamatergic modulation, but did not identify the receptor. A proposed receptor mechanism remained an interpretation, not an established identity.
cards.quote: The pharmacology did not establish the receptor

cards.front: Which channel family, including ASIC subunits, is proposed as a candidate for residual spindle current beyond Piezo2?
cards.back: DEG/ENaC channels; their role is not settled.
cards.quote: Later reviews name DEG/ENaC channels, including ASIC subunits found in spindle endings, as candidates for any current beyond Piezo2's, but their role is not settled.

cards.front: Why need the eight-group and five-group mouse proprioceptor atlases not contradict each other?
cards.back: Labelling, age range, sampling depth and cluster boundaries differ. The group count depends on the data and analysis; cite the study with its count.
cards.quote: They differ in labelling, age range, sampling depth and how clusters were cut.
cards.section: Eight groups, or five: proprioceptor atlases and their disagreement

cards.front: What kind of class does a single-cell RNA-sequencing cluster establish in a proprioceptor atlas?
cards.back: A molecular class, not a proven functional class.
cards.quote: A cluster is a molecular class, not a proven function,
cards.section: Eight groups, or five: proprioceptor atlases and their disagreement

cards.front: Running changed marker-defined Ia subtype composition in mice without changing the total brachial Ia count. Does this prove that neurons converted subtype, and what would help test that interpretation?
cards.back: No. The molecular-class rule means marker-defined groups do not establish stable functional identities. Unchanged total count permits marker regulation or subtype conversion, among other explanations; lineage tracing would help distinguish them.
cards.quote: That could be marker regulation, conversion of subtype, or something else, and lineage tracing would be needed to choose among them.
cards.section: Eight groups, or five: proprioceptor atlases and their disagreement
